section.title: Situation
section.p: Froth is a long-running world of bots, users, messages, tasks, agent cycles, tool invocations, artifacts, deliveries, and observations. Some of these are continuant-like. Some are occurrent-like. Some are temporal entities. Some are observations about the rest.
The current schema style does not express that world clearly. It mixes several habits that are locally convenient but globally confusing:

item.p: thing-centered tables that treat each favored object type as its own little universe
generic link rows whose real meaning is hidden in a predicate string
timestamps attached directly to arbitrary rows as if time were a primitive property of everything
payload blobs that carry distinctions the system actually reasons about
projections that silently become sources of truth

section.p: These choices are not merely aesthetic. They make the system harder to inspect, harder to evolve, and harder to think about coherently. The same relation gets represented in multiple ways. The same temporal structure gets smuggled into local columns. The same underlying entity gets redescribed differently by each subsystem.
Froth needs a more fundamental core: one that treats ontology and relation structure as first-class and lets convenience views be derived from that core rather than substituting for it.

section.title: Goal
section.p: Establish a relational core for Froth that is ontological in structure and operationally useful.
The core should:

item.p: use one neutral table of entities
express important ontology through explicit predicates
treat temporal entities as first-class
treat timestamps as relations to temporal entities rather than as arbitrary inline columns everywhere
treat observations as entities about other entities rather than as a separate metaphysical kingdom
reserve payload blobs for the long tail rather than for core meaning
treat projections and convenience read models as derived and disposable

section.title: Thesis
section.p: Froth should adopt an ontological relational schema built on one neutral items table plus a disciplined family of explicit predicate tables.
In this model:

item.p: items provide the domain of relata
predicate tables carry the real structure of the world
data-property tables relate items to literal values where needed
temporal intervals and instants are items
timestamps attach to temporal entities, not indiscriminately to every other table
payload is residual, not foundational

section.p: The guiding idea is simple: the ontology should live in predicates and a small number of explicit entity types, not in ad hoc foreign keys, not in unstructured JSON, and not in stringly typed link rows.

section.title: 1. Items are neutral entities
section.p: The base table should be minimal:
section.code: items id text/uuid NOT NULL primary key type text NOT NULL payload jsonb NOT NULL default '{}' inserted_at timestamp NOT NULL
section.p: The purpose of items is not to encode the full ontology in one place. It is simply the registry of entities that may participate in relations.

section.title: 2. Ontology lives in predicates
section.p: The real structure of the schema should appear in relation tables. A row in such a table is an assertion of a predicate.
Important predicate families in Froth include:

item.p: mereological predicates such as part_of and temporal_part_of
participation predicates such as participates_in
causal and provenance predicates such as caused_by and derived_from
dependence predicates such as s_depends_on, inheres_in, and concretizes
realization predicates such as realizes
observational predicates such as about
temporal occupancy predicates such as occupies_temporal_region

section.p: Representative tables therefore look like:
section.code: part_of(subject_id, object_id) temporal_part_of(subject_id, object_id) participates_in(subject_id, object_id) caused_by(subject_id, object_id) derived_from(subject_id, object_id) s_depends_on(subject_id, object_id) inheres_in(subject_id, object_id) concretizes(subject_id, object_id) realizes(subject_id, object_id) about(subject_id, object_id) occupies_temporal_region(subject_id, object_id)
section.p: These tables may share a common physical pattern, but they should remain explicit in the schema. A single generic links(predicate, from_id, to_id) table may exist as an escape hatch, but it should not be the primary home of the ontology.

section.title: 3. Data properties are relations too
section.p: Some important predicates connect an item not to another item but to a literal value.
Examples include:
section.code: at_timestamp(item_id, ts) has_status(item_id, value) has_label(item_id, value) has_external_id(item_id, value) has_token_count(item_id, value)
section.p: These are best modeled as tables when the property has stable semantics and operational importance. This keeps meaningful distinctions out of generic payload blobs.

section.title: 1. Continuants and occurrents coexist in the same registry
section.p: Froth contains both continuant-like and occurrent-like entities. Both belong in items.
Examples of continuant-like items:

item.p: messages
artifacts
bots
users

section.p: Examples of occurrent-like items:

item.p: agent cycles
tool invocations
LLM requests
task executions
deliveries

section.p: The schema should not force these into the same object-centered mold. Their differences emerge primarily through predicates.

section.title: 2. Observations are ordinary items
section.p: What software often calls telemetry is best understood here as observation.
An observation is an item that is about another item or process. It is not the primary ontology of the system. It is an entity inside that ontology.
This means spans, log-like observations, measurements, and diagnostic records can be modeled as ordinary items connected by predicates such as about, part_of, or derived_from.

section.title: 3. Dependent entities are allowed
section.p: The schema should leave room for specifically dependent and generically dependent entities where they become useful to model explicitly.
Examples may include:

item.p: a capability or disposition realized in a process
a prompt artifact concretized in a provider request
a model configuration inhering in a session or cycle context

section.p: Not every subsystem needs these distinctions immediately. The point is that the schema should admit them cleanly rather than forcing everything into flattened object tables.

section.title: 1. Temporal entities are first-class
section.p: Temporal instants and intervals should be real items.
An occurrent does not simply own a timestamp. Rather, it occupies a temporal region, and that temporal region is itself an entity in the model.
This yields patterns such as:
section.code:
item type=agent.cycle item type=temporal.interval item type=temporal.instant
occupies_temporal_region(agent_cycle, interval_1) part_of(boundary_1, interval_1) at_timestamp(boundary_1, 1774497814123456)

section.title: 2. Timestamps belong to temporal entities
section.p: The timestamp relation belongs to temporal entities, not directly to arbitrary process rows.
This matters because a calendar datum is not the same kind of thing as a process, a message, or a task. Timestamping is a relation between a temporal entity and a coordinate value.
This does not forbid derived convenience columns or views such as started_at and ended_at. It means those conveniences should be projections, not the primitive truth.

section.title: 1. Payload is residual
section.p: payload remains useful, but its role changes. It should carry:

item.p: raw provider payloads
rare details not worth promoting
unstable experimental fields
migration residue during transitional phases

section.p: If the system regularly reasons over a distinction, that distinction probably belongs in an explicit predicate or data-property table instead.

section.title: 2. Projections are derived and disposable
section.p: The truth model described here will often be join-heavy. That is acceptable.
Operational convenience should come from projections:

item.p: views
materialized summaries
specialized read tables
indexes on high-value predicates

section.p: Examples of good projections in Froth would include:

item.p: current task state
cycle transcript ordering
recent observations for UI inspection
time-bounded process summaries

section.p: The discipline is strict: projections may be optimized and convenient, but they are not the ontological core.

section.title: Example
section.p: A tool call inside an agent cycle could be represented as:
section.code:
items: c1 type=agent.cycle i1 type=tool.invocation r1 type=tool.result m1 type=telegram.message a1 type=artifact o1 type=observation t1 type=temporal.interval u1 type=temporal.instant u2 type=temporal.instant
predicates: temporal_part_of(i1, c1) caused_by(r1, i1) derived_from(m1, r1) participates_in(a1, i1) about(o1, i1) occupies_temporal_region(i1, t1) has_first_instant(t1, u1) has_last_instant(t1, u2) at_timestamp(u1, 1774497814123456) at_timestamp(u2, 1774497815123988)
section.p: This representation distinguishes clearly among the process, its result, an artifact that participates, a message derived from the result, an observation about the process, the temporal interval it occupies, and the calendar coordinates of that interval.
Nothing here requires started_at or ended_at to be primitive fields on the invocation itself. If Froth wants those for query convenience, they can be derived in a projection.

section.title: Migration Strategy

item.p: Introduce items as the common registry for new ontological work.
Introduce a first wave of explicit predicate tables for the relations Froth uses most heavily.
Introduce item-to-literal tables for the properties that are stable and operationally important.
Introduce temporal instants and intervals as items and begin attaching timestamps through them.
Build projections that present the familiar operational surface required by existing tooling and UI.
Gradually retire bespoke linkage and timestamp conventions where the new schema covers them cleanly.

section.p: This transition should be evolutionary. The requirement is not philosophical perfection in one pass. The requirement is that new schema work stop deepening the old confusion.

item.p: Froth gains a more genuinely relational and ontologically legible core.
Parthood, participation, provenance, dependence, realization, and aboutness become explicit.
Temporal reasoning becomes cleaner because temporal entities are represented directly.
JSON payloads shrink back toward the long tail.
New subsystems can be integrated by adding predicates rather than inventing new local universes.
The truth model will often involve more rows and more joins.
The team will need discipline about what becomes an explicit predicate and what remains residual payload.
Good projections will be necessary for hot operational paths.

section.title: Recommendation
section.p: Froth should adopt an ontological relational core built from neutral items, explicit predicates, temporal entities, and derived projections.
The schema should grow by adding meaningful relations rather than by multiplying bespoke object tables or burying semantics in payloads and predicate strings.
This is a better fit for the system Froth actually is: a long-running world of continuants, occurrents, observations, participation, parthood, provenance, and temporal extent.
